items.title: News Analysis: How "China Buffer" anchors a changing Asia-Pacific
text: SHENZHEN, Nov. 17 (Xinhua) -- As energy shocks, shifting trade patterns and an AI-driven technology boom reshape the Asia-Pacific economy, the region's ability to withstand global uncertainties is coming into sharper focus ahead of a key gathering of APEC economic leaders this week.

In this changing landscape, China's industrial strength, vast consumer market and deepening regional ties are emerging as important sources of resilience -- a stabilizing role analysts describe as the "China Buffer."

That role is playing out across the region: Chinese investment is strengthening local manufacturing and technological capabilities; its clean energy exports are helping diversify energy supplies; and China's vast market is opening up new opportunities for regional businesses.

"The 'China Buffer' adds a new dimension to China's relationship with other Asia-Pacific economies," noted Gong Xiaofeng, director of the Institute of Emerging Industry Development in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, Shenzhen University. Long seen primarily as an engine of growth, China is increasingly recognized for its readiness and capability to help the region weather economic shocks, he added.

In Malaysia's Penang, a factory of Shenzhen-based precision manufacturer Keyto offers a glimpse of China's buffering role: it has created jobs, introduced Chinese smart manufacturing practices, and linked local suppliers with China's industrial chains.

Equipped with advanced fluid control technologies used in medical devices, life sciences and environmental monitoring, the facility is helping strengthen Malaysia's high-tech manufacturing capabilities. The company also aims to develop local engineering talent and foster innovation.

Keyto is part of a broader shift. More Chinese companies are establishing production bases across the Asia-Pacific, bringing investment, technology and expertise while integrating deeply with local industrial ecosystems.

In Thailand, Chinese automaker BYD opened a manufacturing plant in Rayong Province in July 2024 and had produced more than 100,000 vehicles as of September 2026. About half of its procurement is sourced locally, while Thai nationals account for 95 percent of its workforce. The plant works with more than 260 suppliers in Thailand and exports vehicles to markets across Asia and beyond.

"China, once seen primarily as a low-cost manufacturing base built on cheap raw materials and labor, is now emerging as a major investor shaping the direction of supply chains and investment landscapes across multiple regions," noted a study released by Thailand's Krungsri Research in August.

Major Chinese electric vehicle and electronics manufacturers in Thailand have attracted upstream suppliers of batteries, semiconductors, electronic components and industrial materials, along with supporting businesses in automation and logistics, creating opportunities for the country to move into higher-value manufacturing and upgrade its technology and clean energy infrastructure, said the study.

items.title: Millennium-old Mazu culture finds new life in the modern era
text: Photo shows a stone statue of Chinese sea goddess Mazu on Meizhou Island, Putian, southeast China's Fujian Province. (Photo/Cai Hao)
The culture surrounding Mazu, the Chinese sea goddess, continues to evolve in the modern era. She is traditionally said to have lived on Meizhou Island in Putian, southeast China's Fujian Province.

Legend has it that Mazu helped fishermen through treacherous waters and died at 28 while saving others at sea during the Song Dynasty (960–1279). Over the centuries that followed, emperors bestowed imperial titles on her 36 times.
Today, some 11,000 Mazu temples in more than 50 countries and regions carry on her legacy. Her values — virtue, benevolence, and universal love — are still taught and celebrated.

Over the centuries, Mazu's role has continued to expand within Chinese folklore. She began as a protector of fishermen caught in storms, then guarded grain convoys on the Grand Canal and ships along the coast, and later watched over trade itself. Envoys carried her on voyages abroad, and overseas Chinese brought her faith with them as a link to home.

Today, her emphasis on helping others has inspired women to pursue their own development. On Meizhou Island, Mazu's birthplace in Putian, a "Digital Mulan" program has run four training sessions for homestay managers, giving 160 rural women free digital skills training. The program has helped tie the island's homestay industry to Mazu culture and coastal tourism.

Photo shows a view of a training session for "Digital Mulan" homestay managers on Meizhou Island in Putian, southeast China's Fujian Province. (Photo courtesy of the Publicity Department of the Communist Party of China Putian Municipal Committee)
Mazu's spirit of benevolence and universal love echoes the values the Red Cross works by: humanity, fraternity and dedication.

At the 2026 Global Mazu Culture Forum, the Fujian Red Cross Foundation and the Meizhou Mazu Charity Foundation jointly launched a charity fund in Mazu's name. Through it, Mazu volunteers will train with the Red Cross in first aid and pass those skills on to their communities.

Mazu, renowned in legend for her knowledge of the skies, now lends her name to a Chinese meteorological warning system. MAZU (Multi-hazard, Alert, Zero-gap and Universal) has been deployed directly in eight countries, including Pakistan, Ethiopia, Jordan and Sri Lanka. More than 50 others use it through a cloud platform.
A charity fund named after Mazu is established during the Global Mazu Culture Forum in 2026. (Photo courtesy of the organizer of the event)

The Mazu satellite, China's first designed to detect sea-surface winds and waves, is in orbit. An upgraded version of the country's ocean forecasting model, MaCOM 2.0, was unveiled recently. The MAZU Scholarship supports exchanges and training for visiting meteorology scholars from Belt and Road partner countries. In Brazil, São Paulo has designated a "Mazu Day," an occasion that has helped make academic exchanges on Mazu culture and maritime civilization between the two countries a regular fixture.
Through such efforts, Mazu culture continues to adapt to the times and benefit people around the world.

items.title: China issues guideline on renewable resources recycling system
text: BEIJING, Nov. 17 (Xinhua) -- Nine Chinese government departments released a guideline aimed at further advancing the construction of the renewable resources recycling system and promoting high-quality development of the recycling industry, the Ministry of Commerce (MOC) said Tuesday.

The document sets out 16 key tasks including promoting the application of typical recycling models, strengthening the recycling and dismantling of solid waste from the products of the "new three," namely electric vehicles, lithium-ion batteries and photovoltaic products, and facilitating quality improvement and upgrading of the recycling sector.

The guideline instructs localities to select and apply typical recycling models suited to local conditions for different categories, including multi-category comprehensive renewable resources, bulky waste furniture and discarded home appliances.

It also makes overall arrangements for the recycling and utilization of solid waste from the "new three" products and calls for addressing weak links in power battery recycling, improving the recycling and utilization system for photovoltaic equipment, and ensuring smooth flows along the entire chain of "design, manufacturing, application, recycling, dismantling and reuse."
The nine departments include the MOC, the National Development and Reform Commission, and the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology.

items.title: Macao targets growth, economic diversification in 2027
text: MACAO, Nov. 16 (Xinhua) -- China's Macao Special Administrative Region (SAR) will seek to maintain economic growth in 2027 and accelerate economic diversification amid downward pressure, Chief Executive Sam Hou Fai said Monday.

Delivering his annual policy address to the Legislative Assembly, Sam outlined plans to attract investment, develop financial services and expand international tourism while maintaining support for residents.

The report identified rising social welfare spending and an excessive reliance on a single sector for fiscal revenue as an unsustainable combination. Macao's economy grew 2.9 percent year on year in real terms in the first three quarters of 2026, according to preliminary figures cited in the report.

To support diversification, the government plans to launch an investment guidance fund, appoint professional fund managers and invest in projects that serve Macao's long-term development. It will seek to attract more projects to Macao and the Guangdong-Macao In-Depth Cooperation Zone in Hengqin.

Financial sector measures include advancing securities legislation, attracting more domestic and overseas companies to issue bonds in Macao, and developing links between the digital pataca and the digital yuan.

In tourism, the government will target markets including Europe, India and the Middle East, offering incentives for flights, hotels and cross-border transport to attract international visitors on multi-destination trips.
The government will also continue its cash-sharing scheme, tax relief and household utility subsidies, and expand free childcare services and support for families.

items.title: Changsha forum: UNESCO official says AI should serve culture
text: Artificial intelligence can help people tell stories about their heritage in new ways, but it is always humans who give those stories meaning, a UNESCO official said at a forum in Changsha, Hunan province, on Monday.

"AI may offer new possibilities for documenting, researching, transmitting and raising awareness of living heritage. But it can also pose risks if cultural knowledge is extracted without consent, if it's misrepresented or if it's treated as data detached from the communities that sustain it," said Shahbaz Khan, director of the UNESCO Regional Office for East Asia.

items.title: Xi meets Chilean president in Shenzhen
text: SHENZHEN -- President Xi Jinping said Tuesday that he is ready to work with Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast to strengthen strategic guidance, keep to the right direction, and jointly draw a blueprint for the growth of bilateral relations, so as to support the development and prosperity of the two countries.

Xi made the remarks during his meeting with Kast in Shenzhen. The Chilean president is in the southern Chinese city to attend the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting, scheduled for Nov 18-19.

Noting that Chile was the first South American country to establish diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China, Xi said the bilateral ties had withstood the test of a changing international landscape and maintained sound and steady development for a long time.
The most valuable experience is that the two sides respect each other, treat each other as equals, and pursue win-win outcomes, he said.

As this year marks the 10th anniversary of the establishment of the China-Chile comprehensive strategic partnership and the 20th anniversary of the entry into force of the China-Chile Free Trade Agreement, the bilateral relations have reached an important juncture for building on past achievements and forging ahead into the future, Xi said.

items.title: Chinese and Russian journalists embark on cross-border media tour to celebrate 30 years of strategic partnership
text: More than 30 reporters from China and Russia kicked off a five-day media tour straddling China's northeastern province of Heilongjiang and the Far East regions of Russia on Sunday.

The event has been held ahead of the seventh China-Russia Media Forum that is set to take place later this month, and is also a celebration of the 30th anniversary of the establishment of the China-Russia strategic partnership of coordination and the 25th anniversary of the signing of the China-Russia Treaty of Good-Neighborliness and Friendly Cooperation.

A total of more than 30 Chinese and Russian reporters will visit the provincial capital of Harbin and the border cities of Suifenhe and Dongning in China before crossing into Russia to report from Ussuriysk and Vladivostok. Their trip will cover academic institutions, high-tech companies, winter sports facilities, trade centers, wild leopard reserves and more, aiming to explore the outcomes and stories of China-Russia cooperation and communication.
The event is cohosted by Heilongjiang Radio and Television Station, the Primorsky Krai branch of the Russian Union of Journalists, and the Far East branch of Rossiyskaya Gazeta.

items.title: Micro-drama turns espionage into a lesson in the law
text: With 59 episodes, each running two to three minutes, the micro-drama Safety Distance has sought to break new ground by using an integrated narrative format to help audiences learn about the law.

Produced under the leadership of the General Office of the Ministry of State Security, with guidance from the Hunan Provincial Department of State Security and the Hunan Provincial Radio and Television Administration, the drama follows state security officers as they investigate espionage cases. Its storylines incorporate elements such as cultural relic restoration, underground black markets and cross-border intelligence contests. Each episode ends with a short legal education video, creating a format that combines drama-driven storytelling with legal awareness, according to the producers.

Recently, the series was selected by the National Radio and Television Administration as one of 14 outstanding micro-dramas for the second quarter. The recognition, some industry observers say, reflects how micro-dramas, once often associated with melodramatic, soap opera-style storytelling, are expanding into more serious subjects.

items.title: Investor sees long-term growth potential in China‘s AI sector
text:
By China Daily | 
          chinadaily.com.cn |
          Updated: 2026-11-17 14:55

The convergence of artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing offers the most promising investment opportunities in China, and the country's ability to turn innovation into industrial strength underpins confidence in its long-term economic outlook, an international investor said.

Yizhou He, managing director and China CEO of Australian Capital Equity, a diversified investment holding group, told China Daily in a written interview while attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation CEO Summit 2026 held on Tuesday and Wednesday in Shenzhen, Guangdong province.

His company has taken equity stakes in Shenzhen-based technology companies. What impressed him most was how closely innovation connects to manufacturing capability, supply chains and real market demand, he said.
On artificial intelligence, He said he would prioritize foundational technologies and infrastructure over standalone a
pplications, which advancing foundation models may increasingly absorb. Breakthroughs can take years of sustained effort with uncertain commercial outcomes, making patient capital important.

He looks at frontier technologies through three tests of reliability, measurable value in real applications and a credible path to a scalable business model. In China, he sees the most promising opportunities where AI meets advanced manufacturing. Core AI technologies and industrial applications reinforce each other, he said, adding that as deployment reveals reliability, data quality and scalability challenges that drive further innovation, China's manufacturing depth carries it to production lines at scale.

In the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, he sees ample potential where Shenzhen's manufacturing strength meets Hong Kong's financial expertise and digital asset ecosystem, including blockchain-based trade documentation and more efficient settlement systems.

Over the next five years, he said, the focus for China is growth quality — "how effectively it can translate scientific and technological advances into higher productivity, stronger industries and globally competitive businesses."

That prospect of industrial renewal underpins his confidence in China's long-term economic outlook, and He said he will keep focusing on businesses with genuine technological strengths and the ability to compete internationally. That depth, he added, will keep opening opportunities for supply chains and investors far beyond China.

Chinese companies expanding overseas can draw on the experience of multinationals that entered China through joint ventures in the past, He said, citing his own earlier experience leading overseas acquisitions. "Headquarters should set clear expectations for governance and risk, while giving local teams meaningful authority to act."

China is hosting APEC for the third time, in a city where ideas move quickly from engineering labs to production lines and global markets, he said. For investors, the value of APEC is often reflected in what happens after the meetings.

items.title: US orchestra praises decades-long exchanges with China
text: When violinist Davyd Booth first traveled to China with the Philadelphia Orchestra in 1973, he couldn't possibly have imagined where the journey would lead.

More than five decades later, Booth is preparing to return with the orchestra for its 14th full-orchestra visit to China. This relationship has evolved alongside the country's remarkable social and cultural transformation.

"Looking back, one had little sense of how historically significant that trip would become," says Booth, 75, who was part of the orchestra's pioneering visit — the first American orchestra to perform in China — under conductor Eugene Ormandy (1899-1985).
"What stood out most was the work with audiences, the public, young people, scholars, and artists."

The Philadelphia Orchestra returns in November for concerts in Haikou, Hainan province, and Beijing, led by its principal guest conductor Marin Alsop, with Chinese pianist Zhang Haochen as soloist. This tour brings together a classical repertoire, from Mozart's Symphony No 40 and Beethoven's Piano Concerto No 5, known as the "Emperor", to Dvořák's Symphony No 7 and Stravinsky's The Firebird Suite.

The tour also features a series of residency activities in Haikou, Shanghai, Beijing, and Shenzhen, Guangdong province, including community performances, educational programs, master classes, and chamber music events.

items.title: 95-year-old American left his heart in Huangyuan, China
text: For 95-year-old American David Plymire, Huangyuan county in Northwest China's Qinghai province remains the place he calls home. Having spent much of his childhood there, he still cherishes memories of its people, local dialect and food. After returning in 1987, he spent decades raising funds to bring more than 30 pieces of medical equipment to the local hospital.
Though he is now too old to make the journey back, the streets, city gates and old friends of Huangyuan remain close to his heart. (Reporter: Mingmei Li; Video: Chelsea Ge)

items.title: Traditional wine finds ways to tempt modern palate
text: In a workshop tucked away deep inside Shaoxing's huangjiu-themed cultural town in Zhejiang province, Liu Xueqin carefully pours a dark, amber liquid into a cup of milk tea. The huangjiu — a traditional rice wine aged for at least 10 years — settles over the tea. She then asks her customers to drink straight from the cup without stirring the concoction to savor the wine's flavor with the very first sip.

Liu's family has been making huangjiu for generations. The 39-year-old remembers being sent to a small shop as a child with a bottle to be filled for her grandfather, who drank it from a bowl at the family table. In autumn and winter, it was mixed with sugar and a beaten egg and warmed.
Huangjiu, despite having been around for centuries, initially had little success with young people, who often found the drink too harsh or bitter for their liking.
Most of Liu's customers were in their 40s and 50s. That is before she began experimenting to make young drinkers like the brew more.

Liu chose milk tea as the bridge, as its sweetness could soften the wine's acerbic edge. Since young people favor sweet drinks, and milk tea is popular, she realized adding huangjiu to it would make the wine palatable.
And the result has proved to be a huge success, she said. Today even her teetotaler customers are not averse to trying the wine-laced tea.

The city's famous amber rice wine no longer just sits in a clay jar beside a plate of autumn crabs. Made mainly from glutinous rice, wheat starter and water, and traditionally aged in clay jars, Shaoxing huangjiu is known for its color and mellow grain aroma.

items.title: China’s Retail Sales Growth Slows to 0.4%, Missing Forecasts
text: China’s retail sales growth slowed to 0.4% year-on-year in October, missing market forecasts as car sales slumped and earlier purchases continued to weigh on demand despite the launch of “Double 11” shopping promotions.
The increase was down 0.7 percentage points from September, data released Monday by the National Bureau of Statistics showed. A Caixin survey of 11 institutions had put average growth at 0.9%.

Car sales remained the biggest drag, falling 21.4% from a year earlier. The decline has widened in recent months, following changes to vehicle trade-in and new-energy vehicle purchase-tax policies. Cars accounted for 7.8% of retail sales in January-October, down from 9.9% for all of 2025.

items.title: China’s Basic Insurance to Cover CAR T-Cell Cancer Therapy
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019275/China’s Basic Insurance to Cover CAR T-Cell Cancer Therapy
text: China will include a CAR T-cell therapy in its national health insurance scheme for the first time, making a blood cancer treatment that once cost over 1 million yuan ($150,000) per dose more accessible.

The National Healthcare Security Administration announced on Nov. 14 that relmacabtagene autoleucel, or relma-cel, made by Shanghai-based biotech firm JW Therapeutics and sold under the brand name Carteyva, will be covered by insurance starting Jan. 1. The therapy has three approved uses for different types of lymphoma and costs 1.29 million yuan per dose.

CAR T-cell therapy is primarily used to treat types of lymphoma and involves extracting and genetically modifying a patient’s own immune cells to target cancer cells, before infusing them back into the body. China approved its first CAR T-cell therapy product in 2021.

Most of China’s population is covered by the country’s national insurance scheme: 1.33 billion were enrolled in basic medical insurance by the end of 2025. Only drugs listed in the national insurance catalog can be partially reimbursed through the medical insurance fund. For drugs not listed, patients must usually bear 100% of the cost.

For years, CAR T-cell drugs were excluded from the national insurance list because an unwritten industry rule held that drugs priced above 300,000 yuan rarely secured coverage, limiting patient access, according to Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper.

The rate of CAR T-cell drug use as a second-line treatment for large B-cell lymphoma in China is about one-sixth of that in the United States, while use as a third-line treatment is about one-10th of the rate in the U.S. and Europe.

Carteyva was one of five CAR T-cell therapies included last year in China’s first commercial insurance list for high-cost innovative drugs. This year, those drugs became eligible for national coverage. Two CAR T-cell drug manufacturers, including JW Therapeutics, entered insurance coverage negotiations on Sept. 6.
“Two or three years ago, we wouldn’t have dared to imagine this,” Tian Feng, JW Therapeutics chairman and CEO, told The Paper.
China records about 101,500 new lymphoma cases each year. Carteyva is available at more than 200 certified hospitals nationwide.

The updated national reimbursement list adds 107 drugs covering oncology, chronic diseases, mental illnesses, rare diseases, and pediatric medications. A separate commercial insurance list, which covers drugs outside the basic scheme, includes 12 new treatments.

“This is a historic moment for lymphoma patients in China,” Tian said, adding that when he and the company received the news, “everyone really felt that the treatment of lymphoma patients in China had entered a new, very exciting era.”

items.title: A Chinese Medical Drama’s Remedy for Big-City Blues: Go Home
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019269/A Chinese Medical Drama’s Remedy for Big-City Blues: Go Home
text: A TV drama about a doctor who returns to his small hometown after being fired from a prestigious city-based position has become a hit among young Chinese, who resonate with its message of finding purpose away from competitive urban areas.

“Small Town Remedy” has been hotly discussed since its Nov. 4 finale. Premiering Oct. 21, the show follows Liu Zhengliang, played by A-list actor Xiao Zhan, a young neurosurgeon who returns to his hometown in northeastern China — or Dongbei — from a major hospital following a botched surgery in which his patient dies.

The show’s popularity comes amid a broader shift in attitudes among young Chinese, who increasingly seek a more sustainable work-life balance and self-care amid growing fatigue stemming from relentless competition and conventional definitions of success.

Socially awkward and unfamiliar with local customs, Liu initially struggles to return to life at home after leaving his post in the southern metropolis of Shenzhen. The series depicts how his brother, childhood friends, and former hospital colleagues gradually help him overcome the trauma of his failed operation, among other personal struggles, such as the death of his mother.

Fans have reported being drawn to the drama’s lighthearted tone and the witty humor commonly associated with China’s Northeast, despite tackling heavy subject matter such as illness, death, and grief.

Its popularity has also sparked an online trend of learning the Dongbei dialect, with video lessons gaining traction on social media. One related hashtag — “‘Small Town Remedy’ Dongbei dialect listening test” — had amassed nearly 1.4 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Monday.

The 29-episode drama has earned an average rating of 8 out of 10 on review platform Douban and reached an audience of 148 million across all streaming platforms, according to data from domestic streaming platform iQiyi. Related hashtags on short-video platform Douyin, China’s version of TikTok, had also garnered more than 8 billion views.

Since the show’s finale, online users have been debating what Liu’s next move should be. Some suggest that as a talented young doctor, he should return to a major hospital to pursue better career prospects, while others say he’d be better off staying in his hometown, where he’d have the emotional space to continue recovering and potentially find greater purpose using his medical skills.

“Everyone wants to go to Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, and Shenzhen, but if life away from home is too difficult, returning to your hometown is not a step backward, nor is it something to be ashamed of,” one user wrote beneath a post discussing the show on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote. “One’s hometown can be a great choice, too.”

“As urbanization continues, more and more young people are facing the same dilemmas as Liu Zhengliang,” another Xiaohongshu user wrote in a comment under the same post, referring to Liu’s struggles with cultural identity and homesickness. “I think the theme of this show really suits the times.”

items.title: Shanghai Sacks Two Scientists Over Child’s Death in Gene Trial
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019274/Shanghai Sacks Two Scientists Over Child’s Death in Gene Trial
text: Shanghai authorities have dismissed two researchers after an investigation into a child’s death following experimental gene-editing treatment found unheeded safety warnings, failures in ethical review, and undisclosed payments and gifts from the family.

The child had Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome, a rare neurodevelopmental disorder with no effective treatment, according to findings released Friday by the Shanghai investigation team. The family contributed 5.3 million yuan ($800,000) toward the research and separately gave researchers approximately 1.06 million yuan in money and gifts.

In July 2023, the family approached Qiu Zilong, deputy director of Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine’s Songjiang Research Institute, hoping his team could develop a customized gene-editing treatment, investigators said.
The child received an injection at the university’s affiliated Xinhua Hospital on March 24, 2025, and died seven days later.
At an emergency review April 2, the hospital’s ethics committee attributed the death to thrombotic microangiopathy, a complication of gene therapy, and ordered the study terminated.

The death went unmentioned in related preclinical research Qiu’s team published in Nature in February 2026, investigators said. The team reported using gene editing to correct a single error in the DNA code of mouse brain cells, restoring levels of a protein essential for normal brain development. The researchers said tests in monkeys also suggested the technique’s potential for use in humans.

Five months later, a joint investigation by Science and Retraction Watch revealed the fatal human trial and reported that the Nature paper had also omitted evidence of liver and kidney damage in animal safety tests.
Shanghai authorities subsequently established a team to investigate the preclinical research, the hospital’s clinical study, and the data underlying the Nature paper.
Investigators found that Qiu’s team had failed to promptly share a safety report from experiments on nonhuman primates with the clinical study’s lead investigator, leaving warning signals unheeded.

Xinhua Hospital’s ethics committee approved the study despite insufficient toxicology and safety evidence, proceeding without additional material it had requested. The hospital also failed to independently and adequately assess the study’s scientific basis and safety.
Investigators said that although the consent form warned the family of serious complications and adverse events, it did not prominently communicate the risk of death.

Investigators found no data fabrication in the Nature paper but identified discrepancies between the research methods used and those described. Data from the same experimental batch had also been presented separately without explanation.

The Nature paper also failed to disclose financial conflicts involving four researchers. Qiu received expensive liquor and electronics worth approximately 100,000 yuan, while Xinhua Hospital associate researcher Yang Kan, the Nature paper’s first and corresponding author, received 900,000 yuan and expensive liquor. Two other members of Qiu’s team each received 30,000 yuan.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: What Made Jade So Valuable in Ancient China and the Americas?
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019256/What Made Jade So Valuable in Ancient China and the Americas?
text: Recent exhibitions at the Shanghai Museum and Beijing’s Capital Museum have introduced Chinese audiences to the civilizations of the ancient Americas. For Chinese visitors, the importance placed on jade may feel familiar. In both ancient China and Mesoamerica, finely worked jade adorned the powerful and accompanied them into the grave, a striking similarity that has long attracted scholarly interest.

How did jade come to carry such authority? One way to explore this question is to compare the jade traditions of Liangzhu and the Classic Maya lowlands, two societies from ancient China and the Americas. Liangzhu was an early regional state near present-day Hangzhou, capital of eastern China’s Zhejiang province, around 3300–2300 BC, with a walled capital, an extensive system of dams, and a pronounced social hierarchy. In the Classic Maya lowlands, spanning parts of present-day Mexico, Guatemala, and Belize, cities ruled by royal dynasties flourished around AD 300–900. Both Liangzhu and Maya cities hold UNESCO World Heritage status.

Thousands of years separated the two societies, and there is no evidence of direct contact between them. Yet both had complex social hierarchies in which powerful ritual authorities played important roles. By tracing jade from the selection of raw stone to its final resting place, we can see how control over labor, knowledge, and materials helped establish its authority in ways that were both similar and distinct.

Jade was valued in both ancient China and the Americas long before Liangzhu and the Classic Maya. The concept of jade encompasses several kinds of stone. Liangzhu’s finest ritual jades were made from nephrite, while Maya jade was principally jadeite. Both were prized for their appearance and could be polished to a lustrous finish. Craftspeople shaped jade using abrasives such as sand mixed with water. Working with different stones helped them recognize differences in hardness and toughness and determine which materials were best suited to particular objects.

In Liangzhu, material choice was closely tied to the form and status of the finished artifact. Other stones, such as serpentine, were generally used for small, less prestigious ornaments. Among the Maya, by contrast, the symbolic meanings of stones were more closely associated with their colors. Green and blue-green evoked water, cultivating maize, and renewed life. Jadeite remained highly prized, but a wider range of similarly colored stones could also be valued for their quality and craftsmanship.
Not everyone had equal access to these raw materials or the specialized skills needed to work them. This inequality helped establish jade’s association with power.

Workshops within and immediately outside Liangzhu city made prestigious ritual objects from nephrite. A short distance away, a large workshop complex specialized in small serpentine ornaments. Despite their proximity, the workshops used different materials and produced different types of objects. The fine finish of these serpentine ornaments, however, shows that their makers were skilled.

items.title: China’s Short Dramas See Quality Shift With AI-Made Historical Hit
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019262/China’s Short Dramas See Quality Shift With AI-Made Historical Hit
text: An AI-generated short drama made by amateurs, including a former rideshare driver and a stay-at-home mother, has gone viral in China for its high production quality and historical accuracy, challenging the genre’s reputation for simple, brainless plots.

First released in August, “Armed Into the Song Dynasty” already has 10 seasons and comprises roughly 1,000 3-minute episodes. As of Thursday, the show has amassed over 12 billion views across platforms including Douyin, China’s version of TikTok, and streaming site Bilibili, local media reported.

In the first nine months of this year, 490,000 micro-dramas were released in China, 13 times more than in all of 2025. AI is also reshaping the micro-drama industry, with AI-generated productions now accounting for more than 90% of all such content, according to a report the National Radio and Television Administration released in October. The report also found that China’s short-drama audience had surpassed 600 million active monthly viewers.

Adapted from a web novel published in installments beginning this April by a writer under the pen name Chagen’er, “Armed Into the Song Dynasty” follows five modern-day soldiers who unwittingly travel back to the late Northern Song dynasty (960–1127), bringing their weapons and military expertise with them.

The late Northern Song period is a popular setting for Chinese time-travel fiction, as it offers viewers an alternative reality to the dynasty’s end, when invading Jurchen tribes captured two of its emperors — widely remembered as a national disgrace.

Fans have praised the drama’s carefully crafted script, elaborate fight scenes, and rounded characters who grapple with everything from the imperial examination system to weapons, food, and military equipment shortages during invasions by northern nomadic groups.
The historical details have prompted some viewers to look up Song-era official ranks, military organizations, and historical records and compare them against the drama’s depictions.

The production team behind “Armed Into the Song Dynasty” reportedly comprises six members — including a former pharmaceutical sales representative, interior designer, rideshare driver, stay-at-home mother, and wholesale business owner — who met during an online course on how to use AI to make short dramas.

Zhang Hansheng, 54, the production team’s head, told domestic media that the series has so far cost roughly 1 million yuan ($150,000) to produce, but declined to disclose the team’s earnings. However, rumors of hefty returns have drawn fresh attention to AI drama production, which many see as a potential source of new opportunities for grassroots content creators.

In the comments on a video interview with Zhang by the domestic outlet Yicai, some viewers said the project had inspired them to learn AI tools and try making dramas themselves. Others urged caution, noting the rise of scams disguised as AI-related courses.

The show’s success comes as the genre shifts toward higher production values. Until recently, short dramas were widely considered mindless entertainment defined by exaggerated interpersonal conflicts, formulaic characters, and implausible plots.

Tracking China’s War of Words Against Japan
text: Beijing is running a concerted campaign to paint Japan as an aggressor and resurgent military threat, according to a Times analysis.

A headline in the Global Times, a newspaper controlled by China’s ruling Communist Party, about Japan’s “remilitarization” after China restricted exports to Japanese entities.Credit...Andy Wong/Associated Press
Javier C. Hernández reported from Tokyo, and Gal Koplewitz from London.
When China’s leader, Xi Jinping, met with President Trump at the White House earlier this fall, the two leaders toasted to friendly relations.

But in private, Mr. Xi offered Mr. Trump a stark warning about Japan, a U.S. ally, according to two officials briefed on the talks, who requested anonymity to discuss private conversations. Mr. Xi told Mr. Trump that Japan’s recent military buildup threatened to destabilize Asia, the officials said, and that Mr. Trump should be cautious about working with Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, describing her as a “militarist.”

The warning from Mr. Xi was part of a broader effort by China to isolate and undermine Japan after Ms. Takaichi said last year that Japan could be forced to defend Taiwan in case of a Chinese invasion. China considers Taiwan, a self-governed democracy that lies just 69 miles from Japan’s westernmost island, part of its territory.

Since the comments, Mr. Xi has overseen a campaign involving propaganda and diplomacy to target Japan, according to interviews with officials and scholars, and an analysis by The New York Times of Chinese Foreign Ministry briefings and state media. It is all part of a push, analysts say, to persuade the world that Japan is a resurgent aggressor.

China has deployed words and images to portray Japan as a World War II-era enemy, using phrases like “remilitarization” and “neo-militarism,” and videos that compare Japan to a “rampaging gray rhino.”

Chinese officials have repeatedly sought to belittle Ms. Takaichi, Japan’s first female prime minister, omitting her title in official briefings, breaking with longstanding practice. State media has depicted Ms. Takaichi in short skirts and a nurse’s uniform in cartoons, and described her as “Abe’s girl,” referring to Shinzo Abe, the former Japanese prime minister and Ms. Takaichi’s mentor.

In private conversations with Western scholars, Chinese academics have recently pushed the narrative that Japan is the “Israel of East Asia,” poised to lead the United States into conflict and destabilize the region.

Russia has helped amplify China’s talking points, branding Japan as a threat. Moscow has echoed Beijing in describing Japan as an “enemy state” that is not to be trusted, invoking a World War II-era designation used against former Axis powers.

Mr. Xi and Ms. Takaichi will cross paths this week at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit meeting in Shenzhen, China. The encounter is expected to be frosty; Mr. Xi might try to use the summit as an opportunity to alienate Ms. Takaichi from Japan’s allies, experts say.
The analysis covered Chinese state-run and Communist Party-run outlets, including China Central Television, the Xinhua news agency, Global Times and People’s Liberation Army Daily.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: Alice Huang’s Husband and the Data-Center Network Backed by China
Mexico keen to strengthen cooperation with China, president says
As Trump Goes to China, A.I. Tensions Surge Amid Spying and Safety Fears
text: When President Trump and Xi Jinping, the leader of China, met earlier this fall, they sounded committed to finding common ground on calibrating the rapid development of advanced artificial intelligence.

“We have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage A.I. for good and ensure that the development of A.I. is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people,” Mr. Xi said in September in the grand foyer of the White House.

Mr. Trump leaned into that spirit, saying, “The decisions we make in these areas today can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come.” But he has called fears of A.I. threats a “hoax,” and earlier that week said at the United Nations that he would label artificial intelligence “super intelligence” to give it a better branding.

On the eve of their third leadership summit of the year, the two men and their administrations have made little if any progress on negotiating A.I. safety issues and development guidelines, despite growing fears about the technology, current and former U.S. officials say.
And that was before Jensen Huang was forced to resign last week as chief executive of Nvidia, the U.S. technology giant that supplies computer chips fueling the A.I. boom.

Mr. Huang stepped down after The New York Times reported last month that the U.S. had gathered intelligence showing that a Chinese businesswoman in Singapore with whom he had a close relationship might have been secretly working or in contact with China’s main spy agency. Mr. Huang has publicly admitted that he had an affair.

Advancements in technology — and particularly on A.I. — have become a focal point in the superpowers’ economic and military rivalry in recent years, but never have those issues been more in the spotlight.

“The primary point of competition between us is certainly on A.I., quantum computing, biotech, cyber, all those issues,” said R. Nicholas Burns, a former career U.S. diplomat who was ambassador to China in the Biden administration.

“But obviously we’ve got a self-interest, and I think they do too,” he added, “in making sure the competition doesn’t veer off in a direction that would be destabilizing and potentially increase the probability of a conflict.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said last week that the governments have had conversations about A.I. safety “sort of at the technical level.” “Obviously, we’ve heard their perspective, they’ve heard ours, but that’s still a work in progress,” he said.
One reason there has been little momentum is that the two nations have differing views of the greatest risks posed by A.I., the current and former U.S. officials say.
In the United States, officials, executives and researchers talk about the possibility of A.I. becoming autonomous and working on its own outside human control or even dominating humans.
That is a concern in China, too, but its government appears to be more worried about how A.I. could be used by humans to undermine the Chinese Communist Party.

items.title: How new US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
text: As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.
On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of  data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.
The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.
South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.

But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.

This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress, a US-based think-tank.
China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".

This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.

One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO.

Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year.

The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands.

The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said.

Countries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University.

items.title: Nvidia warns chip buyers of legal risks tied to China AI access, CNBC reports
text: Nvidia warns chip buyers of legal risks tied to China AI access, CNBC reports             Reuters  Updated Tue, November 17, 2026 at 7:38 AM EST 1 min read                                    NVDA                                Nov 17 (Reuters) - Nvidia (NVDA) said in recent months a proposed US legislation on Chinese ‌companies remotely accessing its artificial intelligence ‌chips could expose it and them to US "legal action," CNBC ​reported on Tuesday, citing sources.
Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
Nvidia stock rose 1% before the bell on Tuesday.

• Nvidia messaged chip buyers in recent months to caution that the proposed ‌Remote Access ⁠Security Act, or RASA, would give the US government broader authority to control ⁠access to cloud services in the same way as physical hardware, the report said
• The chipmaker ​said for ​now it would ​not sell chips ‌to customers who rent over 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs to Chinese companies, the report added
• Nvidia did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment ‌outside regular business hours
• RASA ​is a bill that ​would give the ​US Commerce Department the tools ‌to stop Chinese firms from ​renting overseas ​data centers to access Nvidia chips
• The company said in July that the ​measure, if ‌enacted, could have "a material impact on our ​business"
(Reporting by Gnaneshwar Rajan in Bengaluru; ​Editing by Nivedita Bhattacharjee)

items.title: Trump arrives in Philippines ahead of Xi Jinping summit in China after GOP midterm losses
text: Video  Trump travels to Philippines ahead of historic summit with Xi, Putin Fox News' Mark Meredith reports the latest on his visit from Manila. The Heritage Foundation's Victoria Coates also weighs in on the trip during 'Fox & Friends First.'
President Donald Trump touched down in the Philippines on Tuesday as part of an Asia trip that will take him to China for a historic summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
The trip marks Trump's first overseas visit since Republicans suffered bruising defeats in the U.S. midterm elections.
Trump noted during a gaggle on Monday that while in China this week he will meet with Chinese President Xi Jingping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
TRUMP BRINGS TWO DIVIDED CABINET HEAVYWEIGHTS TO CHINA AS CONTROVERSY HANGS OVER HIGH-STAKES TALKS
President Donald Trump boards Air Force One on Nov. 16, 2026, at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

"And then we go to China. And we'll be with President Xi, he was here a month ago. And we're also gonna meet with President Putin. And we may meet with Kim Jong Un also," Trump said, referring to North Korea's leader. "He may come. I don't know. That's up to President Xi," Trump later added.
Trump indicated that during the meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts, they would discuss issues including denuclearization, Iran, Ukraine, economics and trade.
TRUMP'S ASIA TRIP TAKES ALASKA DETOUR AS WEATHER FORCES REFUELING STOP CHANGE

US President Donald Trump waves U.S. and Philippine flags as he arrives at Ninoy Aquino International Airport to attend the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila on Nov. 17, 2026. (Eloisa Lopez/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

The trip also comes after tech giant Nvidia announced last week that President and CEO Jensen Huang had resigned from the company — the resignation announcement was made after Huang admitted to cheating on his wife amid reporting that he had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
Trump will meet in the Philippines with leaders of the Quad, which includes the U.S., Japan, Australia and India.
He is also slated to engage with leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

He will participate in what’s billed as a "special summit" with the ASEAN leaders, where they are expected to discuss efforts to deepen trade and security ties as well as the region’s longstanding conflicts, including yearslong violence in Burma and escalating disputes in the South China Sea, which Beijing claims virtually in its entirety.
UKRAINE HITS PUTIN'S PRIZED BRIDGE IN RECORD DRONE BLITZ AS KREMLIN TELLS LAWMAKERS TO PREPARE FOR ‘VICTORY’

President Donald Trump gestures upon arriving at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport to attend the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila on Nov. 17, 2026. (Eloisa Lopez/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
Trump is also slated to ink a trade deal with Thailand during his time in the Philippines. He will also meet with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., president of the Philippines.
The Associated Press contributed to this report
Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

items.title: Carney and Xi Announce Canada-China Trade Pact
text: Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada and China’s leader, Xi Jinping, have struck an agreement to reduce some tariffs between their countries, a largely symbolic move that shows relations between the two countries are warming as Canada’s ties to the United States falter.

While the expanded trade between China and Canada resulting from the accord in the Chinese tech and financial hub Shenzhen will be modest, involving just $280 million in exports, the pact — as well as the seemingly amicable meeting — illustrates a contrast to Mr. Carney’s relationship with President Trump. Earlier this year, Mr. Carney said that the United States was “at war” with Canada after trade negotiations between the two countries collapsed in acrimony.

Talks are restarting between Canada and the United States but there is no indication that Washington will back away from key irritants including tariffs of up to 50 percent on Canadian autos, steel and aluminum.

Since entering politics last year, Mr. Carney has been traveling the world to diversify Canada’s economic and political ties away from the United States. Those efforts include current talks to make Canada the European Union’s first associate member and Mr. Carney’s second formal meeting this year with Mr. Xi.

“The stabilization of our bilateral trade arrangement is indicative of how we can work together more broadly, pragmatically, to solve problems,” Mr. Carney said at the start of the meeting with Mr. Xi on Tuesday.
He added that Canada is ahead of schedule with its goal of a 50 percent increase in exports to China by the end of the decade.

China and Canada were in a trade war after the Canadian government under Justin Trudeau, Canada’s former prime minister, followed the lead of the Biden administration and imposed a 100 percent tariff on Chinese-made electric vehicles. China responded with tariffs on a variety of Canadian products, particularly canola, an oil seed.

That dispute was largely resolved in January during the first formal meeting between Mr. Xi and Mr. Carney. China lifted its canola tariff after Canada agreed to allow a relatively small number of Chinese E.V.s into the country at a minimal tariff rate.

Before Tuesday’s meeting, Mr. Xi attempted to put the frosty relations firmly in the past, which were worsened by China’s arrest in 2018 of two Canadians in retaliation for Canada detaining a Chinese telecommunications executive under an extradition request from the United States.

“The development of Chinese-Canadian relations over the years has provided us with an important lesson,” Mr. Xi said at the start of the meeting. “We must respect each other, pursue equality and mutual benefit and seek common ground while setting aside differences.”

Tuesday’s announcement will largely eliminate tariffs on frozen Canadian pork and several seafoods. Both were caught up in China’s E.V. retaliation. Canada, in turn, will continue to suspend tariffs on some Chinese steel and aluminum products that were set to expire at the end of the year. It will also expand the list of products covered by the suspension.

items.title: China, Canada agree to further reduce tariffs at APEC summit in Shenzhen • FRANCE 24 English
Chinese envoy says chip equipment export curbs threaten EU-China trade thaw
Is China Misreading the Moment?
text: RUSH DOSHI is an Assistant Professor at Georgetown University and Director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations. He served as Director and Deputy Senior Director for China and Taiwan Affairs at the National Security Council from 2021 to 2024.
Beijing’s Overreach Threatens the Détente With America

When U.S. President Donald Trump lands in Shenzhen later this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, he will sit down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the fourth time amid an unexpected détente between Washington and Beijing. The trade war of 2025 is in abeyance, the two governments have announced a relationship of “constructive strategic stability,” and, to the alarm of American allies, Trump and Xi are planning to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Beneath the surface, however, the détente is beginning to crack.

The relationship between Washington and Beijing looks remarkably different from the way it did a little over a year ago, when the two sides agreed to a truce in Busan, South Korea.In April 2025, Washington initiated the trade war by raising tariffs on China past 140 percent, and Beijing responded by restricting rare-earth exports later that month and threatening another cutoff that October. After Trump promptly backed down, the two leaders reached the deal in Busan: Washington would cap tariffs and suspend a specific export control regulation known as the Affiliates Rule in exchange for Beijing’s suspension of new export controls on minerals and magnets and the resumption of their normal flow to the United States. On that basis, both sides pursued a broad deescalation.

Since then, the Trump administration has been notably accommodating. Washington has kept new tariffs at 12.5 percent, well below the 20-percent ceiling Beijing previously agreed to. It has let advanced AI chips flow to China and to Chinese cutouts in Southeast Asia and has not added a Chinese firm to the Entity List in over the year, the longest pause since 2008. It has withheld arms sales from and downgraded defense talks with Taiwan, cut back naval transits of the Taiwan Strait, and raised doubts about U.S. support in the event of a crisis. And it has offered only muted support to such allies as Japan and the Philippines in the face of escalating Chinese coercion. All the while, Trump has praised Xi as a “great leader” and extended rare courtesies, including by welcoming Xi on the tarmac when he arrived in Washington for a state visit in September, the first such greeting of a foreign leader in 60 years.

Beijing has appreciated this accommodating approach—and seized the opportunity to act more assertively. It has viewed the competitive pause as temporary, a product of China’s growing strength and Trump’s admiration for Xi, and as a way to buy time to build advantage before the next eruption of tensions. With Washington occupied by its war in Iran and humbled by defeat in the last round of the trade war, Beijing has throttled the supply of minerals and magnets to the United States, taken steps to ensure that its industrial and technological gains remain in China, and increased pressure on its neighbors.
